questions.title: Stages
questions.text:
Put the stages of developing the project database in order:

- **A** Insert test data and check the constraints
- **B** Create the tables with keys and constraints
- **C** Produce the ERD and data dictionary
- **D** Write and test the queries the system needs

scheme.mark_scheme: C, B, A, D (1 each)

questions.title: Constraints
questions.text: Match each constraint to the problem it prevents.

right.text: Two records with the same identifier
A loan for a reader who does not exist
A book saved without a title
Two readers with the same e-mail address

questions.title: Create Book
questions.text: Write the SQL to create the table **Book** with fields ISBN (13 characters, primary key), Title (up to 100 characters, required) and Copies (whole number, at least 0, default 1).

scheme.mark_scheme:
- ISBN CHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY (1)
- Title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL (1)
- Copies INT DEFAULT 1 CHECK (Copies >= 0) (1)

questions.title: Create Loan
questions.text: Write the SQL to create the link table **Loan (ReaderID, ISBN, LoanDate, ReturnDate)**. The primary key is the combination of ReaderID, ISBN and LoanDate; ReaderID refers to Reader and ISBN refers to Book.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- fields with suitable data types (1)
- composite PRIMARY KEY (ReaderID, ISBN, LoanDate) (1)
- FOREIGN KEY (ReaderID) REFERENCES Reader(ReaderID) (1)
- FOREIGN KEY (ISBN) REFERENCES Book(ISBN) (1)
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Loan (
  ReaderID INT,
  ISBN CHAR(13),
  LoanDate DATE NOT NULL,
  ReturnDate DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (ReaderID, ISBN, LoanDate),
  FOREIGN KEY (ReaderID) REFERENCES Reader(ReaderID),
  FOREIGN KEY (ISBN) REFERENCES Book(ISBN)
);

questions.title: Order of creation
questions.text: Explain why the table Loan must be created **after** the tables Reader and Book, and why it must be dropped **before** them.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Loan's foreign keys reference Reader and Book, which must already exist (1)
- the parent tables cannot be dropped while Loan still refers to them (1)
scheme.model_answer: Loan has foreign keys pointing to Reader and Book, so those tables must exist first; and Reader and Book cannot be deleted while Loan still references them, so Loan is dropped first.

questions.title: Data types
questions.text: Choose the most suitable SQL data type for each field: **INT, DECIMAL, VARCHAR, DATE**.

prefill: Price of a book in tenge, e.g. 2450.50

scheme.mark_scheme: DECIMAL (1); DATE (1); VARCHAR (1); INT (1)

questions.title: Phone as text
questions.text: Explain why a phone number is stored as VARCHAR rather than INT.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- INT would lose the leading + / 0 and cannot store spaces / brackets (1)
- no arithmetic is done on phone numbers (1)
scheme.model_answer: An integer would drop the + and leading zeros, and phone numbers are never used in calculations, so text is correct.

questions.title: ALTER TABLE
questions.text: Write SQL statements to add a field **Phone VARCHAR(15)** to the table Reader and then remove the field **Email**.

scheme.mark_scheme: ALTER TABLE Reader ADD Phone VARCHAR(15); (1) ALTER TABLE Reader DROP COLUMN Email; (1)
scheme.model_answer:
ALTER TABLE Reader ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);
ALTER TABLE Reader DROP COLUMN Email;

questions.title: Test plan
questions.text: The field Grade has the constraint **CHECK (Grade BETWEEN 7 AND 12)**. Complete the type of test data and the expected result.

scheme.mark_scheme: 10 normal accepted; 12 boundary accepted; 13 erroneous rejected; 7 boundary accepted (1 per row)

questions.title: Referential integrity
questions.text: Explain what is meant by **referential integrity** and give an example from the library database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- every foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the related table / no orphan records (1)
- example: a loan with ReaderID 99 is rejected if reader 99 does not exist / a reader with loans cannot be deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each foreign key must refer to a record that really exists. For example, a loan for ReaderID 99 is rejected because there is no reader 99.

questions.title: Which insert fails
questions.text: Readers 1 and 2 and book '9780261102217' exist. Which INSERT is **rejected**?

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Reader 7 does not exist — the FOREIGN KEY rejects it.

questions.title: Books on loan
questions.text: Write an SQL query to list the **reader's full name** and the **book title** for all loans that have **not been returned** (ReturnDate is empty), sorted by LoanDate.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- SELECT FullName, Title (1)
- FROM Loan joined to Reader and Book on the keys (1)
- WHERE ReturnDate IS NULL (1)
- ORDER BY LoanDate (1)
scheme.model_answer:
SELECT Reader.FullName, Book.Title
FROM Loan
JOIN Reader ON Reader.ReaderID = Loan.ReaderID
JOIN Book ON Book.ISBN = Loan.ISBN
WHERE Loan.ReturnDate IS NULL
ORDER BY Loan.LoanDate;

questions.title: Project evidence
questions.text: State **two** items of evidence that should be included in the project to show the database was developed and tested.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): CREATE TABLE code / screenshots of table design; relationships diagram; test plan; screenshots of accepted / rejected test data; results of queries
scheme.model_answer: 1 Screenshots of the table designs with keys. 2 The test plan with screenshots showing invalid data being rejected.

questions.title: Clinic database
questions.text: A clinic's new system stores **Doctor (DoctorID, Name, Specialty)**, **Patient (PatientID, FullName, BirthDate, Phone)** and **Appointment (DoctorID, PatientID, AppDate, Room)**. Each doctor has many appointments and each patient has many appointments.

parts.title: Patient table
parts.text: Write the SQL to create the table **Patient**. PatientID is an auto-increment primary key and FullName is required.

scheme.mark_scheme: PatientID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY (1); FullName VARCHAR NOT NULL (1); BirthDate DATE (1); Phone VARCHAR (1)

parts.title: Appointment table
parts.text: Write the SQL to create **Appointment** with a composite primary key (DoctorID, PatientID, AppDate) and the foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme: fields with types (1); composite PRIMARY KEY (1); FOREIGN KEY DoctorID REFERENCES Doctor (1); FOREIGN KEY PatientID REFERENCES Patient (1)
scheme.model_answer:
CREATE TABLE Appointment (
  DoctorID INT,
  PatientID INT,
  AppDate DATETIME,
  Room VARCHAR(5),
  PRIMARY KEY (DoctorID, PatientID, AppDate),
  FOREIGN KEY (DoctorID) REFERENCES Doctor(DoctorID),
  FOREIGN KEY (PatientID) REFERENCES Patient(PatientID)
);

parts.title: Order
parts.text: State the order in which the three tables must be created and explain why.

scheme.mark_scheme: Doctor and Patient (any order) before Appointment (1); Appointment's foreign keys reference them, so they must exist first (1)
scheme.model_answer: Doctor and Patient first, then Appointment, because Appointment's foreign keys refer to the other two tables.

parts.title: Composite key
parts.text: Explain why AppDate is included in the primary key of Appointment.

scheme.mark_scheme: The same doctor and patient can meet many times (1); DoctorID + PatientID alone would not be unique, so the date makes each appointment unique (1)
scheme.model_answer: A patient can see the same doctor more than once, so DoctorID and PatientID together are not unique; adding the date identifies each appointment.

questions.title: Testing the database
questions.text: The field Room in Appointment must be a room number from **1** to **40**.

parts.title: Constraint
parts.text: Write the CHECK constraint for Room (as an integer).

scheme.mark_scheme: CHECK (Room BETWEEN 1 AND 40) / CHECK (Room >= 1 AND Room <= 40) (1)

parts.title: Test data
parts.text: Complete the test plan with one value of each type and the expected result.

scheme.mark_scheme: Normal: any 2–39, accepted (1); Boundary: 1 or 40 (or 0 / 41 as just outside, rejected), result consistent (1); Erroneous: e.g. 55 / -3 / 'A', rejected (1); all expected results correct (1)
scheme.model_answer:
| Type | Value | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | 15 | Accepted |
| Boundary | 40 | Accepted |
| Erroneous | 55 | Rejected |

parts.title: Integrity test
parts.text: Describe a test that checks referential integrity between Appointment and Patient, and the expected result.

scheme.mark_scheme: Insert an appointment with a PatientID that does not exist / delete a patient who has appointments (1); expected: rejected with an error (1)
scheme.model_answer: Try to add an appointment for PatientID 999, which is not in Patient; the DBMS should reject it with a foreign key error.

questions.title: Query
questions.text: The receptionist needs a list of today's appointments.

parts.title: Join query
parts.text: Write an SQL query to show the doctor's name, patient's full name and room for all appointments on **2026-11-20**, sorted by doctor's name.

scheme.mark_scheme: SELECT Doctor.Name, Patient.FullName, Room (1); joins on DoctorID and PatientID (1); WHERE date = '2026-11-20' (accept DATE(AppDate)) (1); ORDER BY Doctor.Name (1)
scheme.model_answer:
SELECT Doctor.Name, Patient.FullName, Appointment.Room
FROM Appointment
JOIN Doctor ON Doctor.DoctorID = Appointment.DoctorID
JOIN Patient ON Patient.PatientID = Appointment.PatientID
WHERE DATE(Appointment.AppDate) = '2026-11-20'
ORDER BY Doctor.Name;

parts.title: Index
parts.text: Explain why an index could be created on AppDate.

scheme.mark_scheme: Searches / sorting by date are faster (1)
scheme.model_answer: Searching for appointments by date becomes faster.

summary: Building the multi-table database of a new system — from the ERD and data dictionary to SQL tables with data types, primary, foreign and composite keys and constraints; creating tables in the right order, changing them with ALTER, adding test data (normal, boundary, erroneous), checking referential integrity, writing multi-table queries and documenting the result.

blocks.content: Developing the database is the step where the **design documents** of a new system become a **working database**. Everything needed is already decided in the design: the **entities** (tables), **attributes** (fields), **data types**, **keys** and **relationships**.

blocks.title: From design to a working database
items: Start from the **ERD** and the **data dictionary** produced in the design stage, normalised to **3NF**.
Choose a **DBMS** (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MS Access) and **create** the database.
Create the tables **in dependency order**: tables **without** foreign keys first.
Add **keys and constraints**: `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES`, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, `DEFAULT`.
Insert **test data** covering **normal, boundary and erroneous** cases and record the results.
Write and test the **queries** the system needs (searches, reports, updates).
**Document** the structure: SQL script or screenshots of the table design, relationships diagram, test evidence.

blocks.title: The project: a school library system
blocks.content:
**Entities:** Book, Reader, Loan. A reader can borrow many books over time, and a book can be borrowed many times → the **many-to-many** relationship is resolved by the **link table** Loan.

```text
  READER ──< LOAN >── BOOK
  (one reader has many loans; one book has many loans)
```

CREATE TABLE Reader (
  ReaderID  INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  FullName  VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  Grade     INT CHECK (Grade BETWEEN 7 AND 12),
  Email     VARCHAR(80) UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE Book (
  ISBN      CHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY,
  Title     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  Author    VARCHAR(60),
  Copies    INT DEFAULT 1 CHECK (Copies >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE Loan (
  ReaderID   INT,
  ISBN       CHAR(13),
  LoanDate   DATE NOT NULL,
  ReturnDate DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (ReaderID, ISBN, LoanDate),                -- composite key
  FOREIGN KEY (ReaderID) REFERENCES Reader(ReaderID),
  FOREIGN KEY (ISBN)     REFERENCES Book(ISBN),
  CHECK (ReturnDate IS NULL OR ReturnDate >= LoanDate)
);
blocks.caption: library.sql — creating the three tables (parents first)

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.content: **Loan** refers to Reader and Book, so Reader and Book must be created **first**. When deleting tables the order is reversed: `DROP TABLE Loan;` **before** `DROP TABLE Reader;` — otherwise the DBMS refuses because Loan still refers to Reader.

blocks.title: Constraints and what they protect
rows: Two books with the same ISBN
**Orphan records** — a loan for a reader or book that does not exist (**referential integrity**)
Repeated values in a non-key field
Two readers with the same e-mail
Empty fields when a sensible value exists

blocks.title: Choosing data types
rows: Leading 0 / + must be kept; no arithmetic

blocks.content:
ALTER TABLE Reader ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);              -- add a field
ALTER TABLE Book MODIFY Title VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL;   -- change a field
ALTER TABLE Reader DROP COLUMN Email;                  -- remove a field
CREATE INDEX idx_title ON Book(Title);                 -- faster searching by title
blocks.caption: Changing the structure later with ALTER TABLE
Inserting normal test data

blocks.content:
INSERT INTO Reader (FullName, Grade) VALUES ('Test Pupil', 13);          -- CHECK fails
INSERT INTO Book (ISBN, Copies) VALUES ('9780000000001', 1);             -- NOT NULL fails
INSERT INTO Loan VALUES (99, '9780261102217', '2026-10-05', NULL);       -- FOREIGN KEY fails
DELETE FROM Reader WHERE ReaderID = 1;   -- fails while Asel still has a loan
blocks.caption: Erroneous tests — each must be rejected

blocks.content: Every **foreign key** value must match an **existing primary key** value in the related table. The DBMS enforces it by **rejecting** inserts of orphan records and **preventing** the deletion of a parent record that still has related child records (or deleting / updating them too with `ON DELETE CASCADE`).

-- 1 Books currently on loan, with the reader's name
SELECT r.FullName, b.Title, l.LoanDate
FROM Loan l
JOIN Reader r ON r.ReaderID = l.ReaderID
JOIN Book   b ON b.ISBN = l.ISBN
WHERE l.ReturnDate IS NULL
ORDER BY l.LoanDate;

-- 2 How many times each book has been borrowed
SELECT b.Title, COUNT(*) AS TimesBorrowed
FROM Loan l JOIN Book b ON b.ISBN = l.ISBN
GROUP BY b.Title;

-- 3 Record a returned book
UPDATE Loan SET ReturnDate = '2026-10-15'
WHERE ReaderID = 1 AND ISBN = '9786010000011' AND LoanDate = '2026-10-01';
blocks.caption: Queries the library needs

blocks.title: Expected result of query 1 for the test data
blocks.content:
| FullName | Title | LoanDate |
|---|---|---|
| Asel Nurlanova | Abai — Book of Words | 2026-10-01 |

Timur's loan is not shown because it has a ReturnDate.

Show: the **CREATE TABLE** code (or table design screenshots) with keys, the **relationships** diagram from the DBMS, the **test plan** with **screenshots** of accepted and rejected data, and the **results** of the main queries.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Write the SQL to create the table Book with ISBN as primary key, Title required and Copies at least 0. [3]**
`CREATE TABLE Book (ISBN CHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY,` (1) `Title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,` (1) `Copies INT CHECK (Copies >= 0));` (1).

**Q: Explain why the table Loan must be created after Reader and Book. [2]**
Loan contains **foreign keys** that **reference** Reader and Book (1); the referenced tables / primary keys must **already exist** (1).

**Q: Explain how a foreign key keeps the data consistent. [2]**
A loan can only be added if the ReaderID / ISBN **exists** in the parent table (1), so there are **no orphan records** — referential integrity (1).

**Q: Give one item of erroneous test data for Grade and the expected result. [2]**
Grade **13** (or "eleven") (1) — **rejected** by the CHECK constraint / error message (1).

- Creating a table with a **foreign key before** the table it refers to.
- Storing **phone numbers** as INT (loses the leading + / 0).
- Forgetting the **composite primary key** in a link table.
- Testing only normal data — always include **boundary** and **erroneous** data.
